lessons.title: The JavaScript Workbench
lessons.subtitle: Build a repeatable edit, run, inspect, explain loop.
objectives: Separate the JavaScript language from its host environment.
Run and inspect a small program in a browser and Node.js.
Use predictions and evidence to debug a program.

body.heading: One language, several environments
paragraphs: JavaScript defines values, expressions, objects, functions, and other language behavior. A host environment supplies additional capabilities. A browser provides a document and browser events; Node.js provides access to processes and files. The same arithmetic expression behaves similarly in both, but document.querySelector is a browser capability. Treating this distinction as a boundary helps you understand unfamiliar examples instead of memorizing where each function happens to work.

Create a scratch directory with one JavaScript file and one HTML file that loads it. Keep experiments small enough to inspect completely. Record how you ran each example, the expected output, and the actual output. When a name is missing, first identify whether it belongs to your code, the language, or the host. That question is often more useful than immediately changing syntax.

body.heading: Read programs as a sequence of observations
paragraphs: Before running a snippet, predict its result in writing. Then execute it and compare your prediction with the evidence. A useful explanation names the values at each step and the operation that transforms them. Console output is one form of evidence; a breakpoint lets you inspect the same state without adding permanent logging. Neither technique replaces reasoning about which instructions have actually executed.

Make a deliberate mistake, such as misspelling a variable, and inspect the resulting error. Identify the error type, the source location, and the first stack frame in your own code. Correct one cause at a time and rerun the smallest reproduction. This process develops a portable debugging habit: observation, hypothesis, isolated change, and confirmation. Keep a short notebook of mistaken predictions and their explanations.

body.heading: Build the first useful slice
paragraphs: Your first program should have an observable result and a deliberately limited scope. A study-session estimator is enough: accept a number of lessons and minutes per lesson, compute a total, and present it clearly. Separate calculation from presentation even in this small example. A function that returns a number can later be used by a command-line interface, a browser page, or a test.

Write down assumptions before adding features: are fractional lessons allowed, can minutes be negative, and what should happen with missing input? You do not need an elaborate architecture to make these decisions explicit. Finish by explaining your program to an imaginary reviewer using concrete inputs. If the explanation requires guessing what a variable contains, improve the name or inspect the value before continuing.

pitfalls: Assuming every global function is part of the JavaScript language.
Making several unrelated edits before rerunning a failing example.

quiz.question: Which capability is supplied by a browser host?
quiz.explanation: The DOM document is a browser API; arrays, operators, and functions are language features.

quiz.question: What is the most useful next step after an unexpected result?
options: Reduce the example and inspect intermediate values
Ignore it if the page renders
quiz.explanation: A small reproduction makes the causal chain visible and lets you test one hypothesis at a time.

lessons.title: Values, Types & Identity
lessons.subtitle: Know what a variable contains and what an assignment copies.
lessons.chapter: Ch. 2–3 · Lexical Structure; Types, Values, and Variables
objectives: Distinguish primitive values from object references.
Choose explicit conversions for boundary inputs.
Explain const bindings, mutation, and equality.

body.heading: Values are the starting point
paragraphs: JavaScript values have types even though a variable can hold different types over its lifetime. Common primitive types include number, string, boolean, undefined, null, bigint, and symbol. Objects include arrays and functions. A missing property typically evaluates to undefined; null is often an intentional marker selected by an API. These are different signals, so define what each means in your own program rather than treating every empty-looking value identically.

Input boundaries deserve special attention because form controls and command-line arguments commonly provide strings. The text "12" and the number 12 can participate in different operations. Convert deliberately, then validate the result with a check that matches your requirement. Number.isFinite rejects NaN and infinities without coercion. An empty string converts to zero with Number, which may be inappropriate for a required field.

body.heading: Bindings are not containers that freeze objects
paragraphs: A variable binding associates a name with a value. const prevents reassignment of that binding; it does not make an object immutable. When two variables refer to the same object, changing a property through either name affects the same underlying object. By contrast, assigning a primitive gives another binding access to that immutable value, and later reassignment does not change the other binding.

Draw arrows when reasoning about identity. For const first = { score: 1 }; const second = first;, draw two names pointing to one object. For a spread copy, draw another outer object, but remember that nested objects are still shared. This visual distinction explains many surprising updates in application state. Decide whether a function may mutate its arguments and make that decision part of its contract.

body.heading: Conversions need a policy
paragraphs: Strict equality compares values without the coercion rules of loose equality. For objects, equality means identity, not matching contents. Two separately created arrays are different even when their elements look identical. Numeric calculations introduce another consideration: JavaScript numbers use floating-point representation, so some decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly. Compare calculated measurements using a tolerance appropriate to the problem instead of expecting every decimal result to be exact.

Keep lexical details clean while practicing these ideas: use descriptive identifiers, consistent punctuation, and strings whose quoting is easy to inspect. Separate raw input, converted values, and validated domain values with different names. Write a tiny table covering empty text, numeric text, invalid text, zero, and negative numbers. The table becomes a specification for your conversion policy and reveals whether the program accidentally accepts missing input.

pitfalls: Reading const as a promise that an object cannot change.
Using truthiness to validate a number when zero is a legitimate value.

quiz.question: What does const settings = { dark: false } prevent?
quiz.explanation: const protects the binding; the referenced object remains mutable unless other measures are applied.

quiz.question: What is the result of [] === []?
quiz.explanation: Each array literal creates a distinct object, and strict equality compares object identity.

lessons.title: Expressions That Tell the Truth
lessons.subtitle: Make operators, defaults, and short-circuiting explicit.
objectives: Trace operator precedence and evaluation order.
Choose between logical OR and nullish defaults.
Write readable conditional and property-access expressions.

body.heading: Expressions produce values and may do work
paragraphs: An expression evaluates to a value, but evaluation can also cause observable effects. A function call might write a log, mutate state, or start a request. Arithmetic, property access, comparisons, and assignments are all expressions with different rules. Operator precedence determines grouping; evaluation order determines when operands are evaluated. Parentheses make the intended grouping visible without requiring a reader to remember the entire precedence table.

Consider total = price + fee * quantity. Multiplication groups more tightly than addition, which may or may not match the business rule. Name intermediate values when an expression mixes several concepts. The goal is to expose the domain calculation: unit cost, subtotal, discount, and final amount. A few clear assignments often communicate more effectively than a compressed formula with several nested conditional operators.
body.code:
const unitCost = price + fee;
const subtotal = unitCost * quantity;

body.heading: Short-circuit operators return operands
paragraphs: The logical operators && and || select and return operand values; their results are not necessarily booleans. Evaluation may stop before the right operand runs. This allows compact checks but can hide side effects. The nullish coalescing operator ?? selects its fallback only for null or undefined, whereas || uses the broader category of falsy values. The distinction matters whenever zero, false, or an empty string is meaningful.

Build a small truth table for a setting such as playbackVolume. If zero means mute, volume || 50 changes a valid choice into a default. volume ?? 50 preserves it. Write the table before choosing an operator, and include absent values and valid edge values. When mixing nullish and logical operators, use explicit parentheses as required by the syntax and to make the policy immediately readable.

body.heading: Read safely without disguising invalid state
paragraphs: Optional chaining stops a property-access or call chain when the relevant receiver is null or undefined. It is useful when absence is expected, such as an optional profile. It does not validate the object, catch arbitrary exceptions, or guarantee that a present property has the right type. A required configuration value should usually be checked explicitly rather than silently replaced after every failed access.

Use a conditional expression for a simple choice between two values, and use statements when the branches perform several actions. Prefer boolean names such as isComplete when you need a boolean result. When reading unfamiliar code, annotate each expression with the value it returns and whether it can skip work. This discipline exposes accidental assignments in conditions, unexpected string concatenation, and defaults that erase legitimate values.

pitfalls: Assuming && and || always return true or false.
Using optional chaining everywhere and concealing a broken required invariant.

quiz.question: Which expression uses 10 only when value is null or undefined, while preserving a valid zero?
quiz.explanation: Nullish coalescing falls back only for null and undefined, so it preserves zero.

quiz.question: What does false && expensiveOperation() do?
options: Calls the function and returns false
Skips the function and returns false
quiz.explanation: Logical AND short-circuits when its left operand is falsy.

lessons.title: Decisions & Defensive Control Flow
lessons.subtitle: Turn vague requirements into complete branches.
objectives: Translate rules into mutually understood branches.
Use guard clauses and explicit failures.
Distinguish expected outcomes from exceptions.

body.heading: A branch is a decision table in code
paragraphs: An if statement chooses which statements execute based on a condition. The challenge is usually not syntax but defining complete rules. Consider a course enrollment request: the course may be closed, the user may already be enrolled, or a seat may be available. Write these cases as a decision table, including their precedence. Otherwise the code may accidentally choose a convenient condition instead of the intended business outcome.

Use braces consistently so the scope of each branch is visible. Add boundary examples before implementing comparisons: exactly zero seats, exactly the minimum age, or exactly the deadline. These examples reveal whether the operator should be less than or less than or equal. When a condition becomes difficult to explain aloud, name it or extract a small predicate rather than adding another nested expression.

body.heading: Guard clauses make the main path visible
paragraphs: A guard clause handles a special or invalid situation near the beginning of a function and exits early. This can keep the successful path at a consistent indentation level. It is especially effective at boundaries where raw input must satisfy a few clear requirements. The order of guards is part of the behavior: if several rules fail, the first guard determines which result or error the caller receives.

Do not confuse concise guards with incomplete validation. Decide whether a rejected request should return a structured result, return a sentinel value, or throw an exception. Expected user mistakes often work well as explicit results; violated programmer assumptions may justify exceptions. Whichever policy you choose, make the caller handle it consistently and ensure that no partial mutation happens before the validation finishes.

body.heading: Choose branching structures for the domain
paragraphs: A switch statement is useful when one expression is compared against a fixed set of cases. Without a terminating statement, execution can continue into subsequent cases; this fallthrough should always be intentional and obvious. A lookup object may be clearer for a pure mapping, while if statements suit ranges and compound conditions. Select the structure that makes missing cases easy to notice during review.

Finish every decision function by looking for an unhandled situation. Unknown statuses, malformed values, and impossible combinations deserve explicit behavior. Test each branch using a representative example and test the boundaries between branches separately. This is more informative than repeatedly testing the common success path. Write the expected result before running the function so a surprising output cannot quietly become the new specification.

pitfalls: Validating after changing shared state.
Forgetting switch fallthrough or leaving unknown values undefined.

quiz.question: What should happen before mutating an enrollment record?
options: Convert every value to a boolean
quiz.explanation: Validation should precede mutation so rejected input cannot leave partially changed state.

quiz.question: Which test is most likely to expose an incorrect <= comparison?
quiz.explanation: Boundary tests distinguish inclusive from exclusive comparisons.

lessons.title: Loops, Collections & Invariants
lessons.subtitle: Make repetition correct, bounded, and explainable.
objectives: Choose a loop based on its stopping condition.
Explain loop invariants and off-by-one errors.
Use break and continue without hiding behavior.

body.heading: Every loop needs a progress argument
paragraphs: A loop repeats work while a condition permits it. A useful explanation includes the initial state, the work performed, the state change, and the reason repetition eventually stops. For a counted loop, the index approaches an upper bound. For a search, the collection is exhausted or a match ends the loop. If you cannot identify a progress measure, the program may repeat forever on an unexpected input.

Start with the smallest collections: empty, one item, and two items. These cases make off-by-one mistakes visible. Prefer a half-open index range from zero up to but excluding length when indexing an array. Decide whether you need an index at all; for...of directly visits values of an iterable. Keep loop state close to the loop so the reader can see what controls termination.

body.heading: An invariant explains why the result is trustworthy
paragraphs: A loop invariant is a statement that remains true before and after each iteration. When summing durations, the accumulator equals the sum of all items already processed. It begins at zero, each iteration adds exactly the next duration, and at termination every item has been processed. This style of reasoning makes correctness concrete and exposes duplicate processing, skipped values, and accidental resets inside a loop.

Write an invariant in a comment for your first few algorithms. Then trace one input in a table with columns for the index, current value, and accumulator. Include a negative value or another edge case if the contract permits it. The purpose is to connect the implementation to a claim you can verify, rather than assuming that a plausible-looking loop must be correct.

body.heading: Early exits are part of the contract
paragraphs: break stops the nearest enclosing loop, while continue skips the remaining work in the current iteration. Both can express useful rules, such as finding the first matching lesson or ignoring a canceled session. They can also obscure the relationship between counters and processed records. Decide whether your result describes all input, only valid input, or the prefix before an early exit, and name it accordingly.

Do not use for...in as a substitute for value iteration over arrays; it enumerates property keys and brings a different set of semantics. Avoid modifying a collection while traversing it unless you have reasoned about how the iteration sees changes. For an initial implementation, accumulate a new collection and keep the source stable. Make any intentional mutation visible in the function name or documentation.

pitfalls: Using an inclusive upper bound with a zero-based array index.
Updating a progress counter only on some paths through the loop.

quiz.question: Which indexed loop covers an array without reading past its end?
quiz.explanation: Valid indexes range from zero to length minus one, so the upper bound is exclusive.

quiz.question: What does continue do?
options: Skips to the next iteration of the nearest loop
quiz.explanation: continue skips the rest of the current iteration and proceeds according to the loop mechanics.

lessons.title: Scope, Errors & Small Programs
lessons.subtitle: Combine the fundamentals into a dependable command.
objectives: Explain lexical scope and temporal dead zones.
Propagate errors with useful context.
Deliver a small program with explicit input and output contracts.

body.heading: Scope determines where a binding can be used
paragraphs: Lexical scope is determined by the structure of source code. A binding declared inside a block with let or const is available within that block and its nested scopes, subject to initialization rules. A same-named inner binding shadows an outer one. This can be useful, but unnecessary shadowing makes debugging harder because a familiar name may refer to a different value at a different location.

Declarations with let and const have a temporal dead zone before initialization. Access during that interval throws rather than returning undefined. Avoid relying on declaration quirks: declare values near their first meaningful use, prefer narrow scopes, and use distinct names when they represent different concepts. These habits reduce the amount of program state you must mentally track while reviewing a function or investigating a failure.

body.heading: Errors should preserve the useful story
paragraphs: Throwing an error transfers control until an appropriate catch handler is found. Use an Error object so the failure carries a name, message, and stack trace. A catch block should recover, translate the failure at a boundary, or add useful context before rethrowing. Catching everything and returning an arbitrary default can turn a clear failure into corrupt output that appears successful to its caller.

A finally block runs when leaving the try statement, including many abrupt exits, and is useful for cleanup. Avoid returning from finally because that return can replace an earlier result or exception. At the application boundary, present a concise message and retain diagnostic details for debugging. Within calculation functions, keep failures precise enough that a caller can distinguish invalid input from a defect in the implementation.

body.heading: Deliver a complete small slice
paragraphs: Build a study-plan calculator that accepts lesson counts and time estimates, computes a schedule, and returns a structured result. Keep parsing, validation, calculation, and display as separate responsibilities. This separation is useful even before modules: each part can be called with a small example. Define whether the program rounds up sessions, permits zero available minutes, and treats an empty plan as valid input.

Use a short acceptance checklist: normal inputs produce expected totals, boundary inputs have specified behavior, invalid inputs fail clearly, and no hidden global state changes the result. Add a README-style explanation in your own notes with one successful example and one rejected example. Review the program by tracing a value from raw input to final output, identifying the contract at every transition. This is your first miniature engineering review.

pitfalls: Using a catch block to hide errors without a recovery policy.
Returning from finally and accidentally overriding a thrown error.

quiz.question: What happens when a let binding is read before initialization in its scope?

quiz.explanation: The binding exists but is in its temporal dead zone until initialization.

quiz.question: Where should a friendly user-facing error usually be created?
quiz.explanation: The boundary can translate internal failures into an appropriate presentation while preserving diagnostic context.

lessons.title: Objects as Models
lessons.subtitle: Give records clear meaning and predictable update rules.
objectives: Model records using intentional property names.
Distinguish property absence from an undefined value.
Perform shallow updates without misunderstanding nested references.

body.heading: A record is a set of domain decisions
paragraphs: An object groups properties under a single identity. Before writing a literal, decide what the record represents and which properties are required. A lesson record might contain id, title, durationMinutes, and status. Names encode units and meaning; durationMinutes prevents confusion that a generic duration invites. A stable identifier lets other records refer to a lesson without depending on a title that may change during editing.

Property keys are strings or symbols, and bracket notation evaluates an expression to choose a key. Dot notation is convenient for a known identifier-like name. When a key comes from input, validate it against the operation you intend to support. A general-purpose object updater that accepts every possible property is harder to reason about than a small operation such as renameLesson or completeLesson.

body.heading: Presence and value are different questions
paragraphs: Reading a missing property usually returns undefined, but an existing property can also hold undefined. The in operator checks whether a property exists anywhere along the prototype chain. Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(record, key) checks an own property and works even when the record has a conflicting property name. Choose the question that matches the contract rather than treating all these checks as interchangeable.

Enumeration also has specific rules. Object.keys returns enumerable own string keys; it does not include every possible property. Object.entries is useful when processing a record as pairs. Keep data records simple while learning: avoid mixing arbitrary inherited behavior into objects that are primarily serialized data. Make optional properties intentional and document whether omission, undefined, or null represents the absence your application needs.

body.heading: Updates need an ownership policy
paragraphs: Object spread creates a new outer object and copies enumerable own properties. It does not recursively clone every referenced object. If a record contains a nested progress object, both copies may still share it. An immutable nested update must copy each object along the changed path, or use a different data layout that reduces nesting. The right choice depends on the size and complexity of the model.

Write operations that return a new record when callers should retain the previous snapshot. Alternatively, explicitly allow mutation when one component owns the record exclusively. What causes trouble is an undocumented mixture of both policies. Check updates with assertions about both values and identity: the changed record should contain the new value, the previous record should remain correct, and intentionally unchanged branches may still share references.

pitfalls: Confusing property absence with a present undefined value.
Assuming object spread recursively copies nested records.

quiz.question: What does {...record} create?
options: A shallow copy of enumerable own properties
quiz.explanation: Spread copies the outer properties; nested references are still shared.

quiz.question: Which check includes inherited properties?
quiz.explanation: The in operator searches the prototype chain as well as own properties.

lessons.title: Arrays as Data Pipelines
lessons.subtitle: Express selection, transformation, and aggregation clearly.
objectives: Choose map, filter, find, and reduce by intent.
Control mutation when sorting or editing arrays.
Handle empty and sparse collections deliberately.

body.heading: Choose an operation that explains the result
paragraphs: An array is an ordered collection whose elements are accessed by numeric indexes. A pipeline becomes readable when each operation describes a distinct transformation. filter selects elements, map produces one output for each visited element, find returns the first match, and reduce accumulates a result. Begin by writing the desired input and output shapes. Then choose operations that communicate how one shape becomes the other.

Do not use map simply to perform side effects while discarding its returned array. A loop or forEach states that intention more clearly. A long pipeline can also become obscure when callbacks mix filtering, mutation, and logging. Name meaningful intermediate collections during development. Clear stages make it easier to inspect an unexpected result and isolate whether selection, conversion, or aggregation introduced the error.

body.heading: Order and mutation are part of the contract
paragraphs: Methods such as sort, reverse, splice, push, and pop mutate their receiver. Other methods return a new array. If callers retain earlier snapshots, copy before using a mutating operation. A numeric sort requires a comparator such as (a, b) => a - b; the default sort compares string representations. For records, define a primary key and a tie-breaking rule when deterministic ordering matters.

An array copy still shares object elements. Sorting a copied array preserves the source order, but mutating an element in the copy may affect the source record. Test these as separate concerns: array identity, element identity, order, and property values. The distinction becomes central when a user interface stores snapshots or a function promises to leave its input unchanged for later comparison.

body.heading: Empty input is a real input
paragraphs: An empty collection should have an explicit result. Summing zero durations naturally gives zero, so provide an initial accumulator to reduce. Finding a missing record returns undefined. Computing an average requires an additional policy because dividing an empty total by zero does not produce a meaningful domain value. Do not let an incidental arithmetic result decide how the product represents missing information.

Sparse arrays contain missing indexes, which differ from indexes explicitly holding undefined. Different operations can observe holes differently, making sparse arrays a poor default for application collections. Build dense arrays by appending actual records or mapping well-defined sources. For every pipeline, include empty input, one element, duplicates, and invalid records in your review. Explain whether invalid records are rejected or excluded, and avoid silently changing that policy between steps.

pitfalls: Sorting numbers without a comparator.
Calling reduce without an initial value when the collection may be empty.

quiz.question: Which operation returns the first matching value?
quiz.explanation: find returns one matching element or undefined; filter returns an array.

quiz.question: How can you sort numeric values without changing the source order?
quiz.explanation: The spread makes a new outer array and the comparator performs numeric ordering.

lessons.title: Functions & API Contracts
lessons.subtitle: Design callable units that are easy to trust and test.
objectives: Write explicit parameter and return-value contracts.
Separate pure calculations from observable effects.
Choose function forms for clarity and behavior.

body.heading: A function is a promise to its caller
paragraphs: A function contract states accepted inputs, the returned value, possible failures, and observable effects. For calculateCompletion(completed, total), decide whether total may be zero, whether fractions are allowed, and whether completed may exceed total. Without these rules, even a two-line function is ambiguous. A good name narrows the promise, and a concise comment records details that cannot be inferred from the name alone.

Implement the smallest function that fulfills one promise. If a function parses input, updates storage, renders a message, and calculates a percentage, failures become difficult to isolate. Split responsibilities at useful boundaries, not at arbitrary line counts. A slightly longer function with one coherent purpose is often easier to understand than several tiny helpers whose names do not explain why they exist.

body.heading: Pure functions are convenient test surfaces
paragraphs: A pure calculation depends only on its inputs and produces no externally visible mutation. Calling it with equivalent inputs yields equivalent results, which makes examples easy to reproduce. Effects such as reading the current clock, writing storage, and modifying the DOM are still necessary, but can sit outside the calculation. Pass needed environmental values as arguments so the core decision remains deterministic.

For a deadline checker, supply now rather than calling Date.now deep inside the rule. For a recommendation function, pass the lessons instead of reading a global array. These changes make the hidden dependencies visible. Test both the returned value and the promise that input objects remain unchanged. Purity is a design tool, not a requirement for every function; effectful functions should simply make their responsibilities explicit.

body.heading: Function forms carry different semantics
paragraphs: Function declarations, function expressions, and arrow functions can all describe callable behavior, but they are not interchangeable in every situation. Declarations have useful initialization behavior within their scope. Arrow functions use lexical this and do not provide their own arguments object. A concise arrow body returns its expression; a block body requires an explicit return when a value is intended.

Choose a consistent form for the role, and optimize for the next reader. A named function improves stack traces and explains a substantial operation; a short arrow works well as a local transformation callback. Watch for implicit undefined when a branch forgets to return. Build a contract table containing normal cases, boundary cases, and rejected cases, then use it to assess every path through the implementation.

Forgetting return inside an arrow function with a block body.

lessons.title: Closures & Higher-Order Functions
lessons.subtitle: Use captured state and behavior as deliberate building blocks.
objectives: Explain what a closure captures.
Build a stateful function factory with controlled ownership.
Use higher-order functions to compose behavior.

body.heading: Functions retain access to lexical bindings
paragraphs: A closure combines a function with access to the lexical environment where it was created. The function can continue using those bindings after the outer call has returned. It captures access to bindings, not a frozen snapshot of every value. If a captured binding changes, a later call observes the current value. This explains both useful private state and confusing behavior in callbacks created around shared mutable variables.

Trace a factory by drawing one environment for each invocation. Two calls to makeCounter create independent count bindings, while two references to the same returned function share one environment. Block-scoped let in a loop gives callbacks the expected per-iteration binding in common patterns. Practice predicting these relationships before executing the code; the model is more durable than memorizing a closure definition.

body.heading: Private state still needs a clear contract
paragraphs: A function factory can expose a small API while keeping implementation state out of direct reach. A study timer might expose start, pause, and elapsed functions that share one private state. The absence of public properties does not automatically make the design correct: you still need valid transitions, clear ownership, and behavior for repeated calls. Closure-based encapsulation is useful when it reduces the number of states callers can create.

Be careful about retaining large objects through long-lived closures. A registered callback may keep its environment reachable even after a screen disappears. Define a cleanup path for subscriptions and timers when the surrounding component owns them. During testing, create fresh factories for independent cases so captured state does not leak between tests and make outcomes depend on execution order.

body.heading: Behavior can be passed like other data
paragraphs: A higher-order function accepts functions, returns functions, or both. Array methods are familiar examples, but you can also build reusable policies such as withLogging, once, or a predicate combiner. Keep the wrapped function contract intact: preserve argument handling, returned values, and thrown errors unless the wrapper explicitly promises to change them. Otherwise a useful-looking abstraction can subtly break the caller.

Start with a small composition exercise: trim a string, normalize case, and validate the result using separate functions. Name intermediate behavior when it improves readability. Avoid building a generic functional framework before a real repetition appears. The purpose of higher-order functions is to express reusable behavior clearly, and the best abstraction is usually the smallest one that removes an actual duplication in your program.

pitfalls: Thinking a closure captures an immutable copy of a variable.
Sharing one factory instance across tests that should be independent.

quiz.explanation: Each invocation creates its own environment, retained by its returned closure.

quiz.question: A wrapper that calls a function but omits return changes what?
quiz.explanation: Callers receive undefined instead of the wrapped function result.

lessons.title: Parameters, Context & Composition
lessons.subtitle: Make invocation behavior explicit at every call site.
objectives: Use defaults, rest parameters, and destructuring intentionally.
Explain this according to invocation style.
Compose functions without hiding dependencies.

body.heading: Parameters are the front door of an API
paragraphs: Default parameters apply when an argument is omitted or explicitly undefined, not when it is null. Rest parameters collect remaining arguments into an actual array. Destructuring can make an options object readable and reduce positional ambiguity. For example, schedule({ minutes, breakMinutes = 5 }) communicates more clearly than schedule(25, 5, true, false), especially when several values share the same primitive type.

Defaults should encode a product decision rather than conceal required input. If a course identifier is mandatory, a fallback identifier may route work incorrectly instead of helping. Validate options after applying legitimate defaults, and decide how unknown properties are handled. A small options object is often enough; avoid allowing every internal detail to become a public option because each option creates a contract you must maintain.

body.heading: The call site determines ordinary this
paragraphs: For an ordinary function, this depends on how it is called. A method invocation such as timer.start() supplies the receiver as this. Extracting const start = timer.start and calling start() loses that receiver. In strict mode, a plain function call has undefined this. Arrow functions behave differently: they inherit this from the surrounding lexical environment instead of receiving it from a method call.

Use bind when you intentionally need a function permanently associated with a receiver, or use a small closure that makes the intended call explicit. Do not automatically bind every method; first ask whether the operation needs this at all. Passing data as a parameter can be clearer for reusable calculations. Predict the receiver at the call site before interpreting a method body that reads properties through this.

body.heading: Composition makes dependencies visible
paragraphs: Composition builds larger behavior by combining smaller functions with compatible contracts. A parsing function can produce a validated count, which a planner turns into a schedule, which a formatter turns into text. The boundaries work when each output shape matches the next input shape. If each step catches failures differently or mutates shared state, a neat pipeline can hide a difficult execution model.

Document the intermediate values for one complete example. Then inject a failure at each boundary and trace who handles it. This reveals whether errors are duplicated, swallowed, or translated too early. Prefer a clear sequence of named steps to an elaborate compose utility until repetition justifies the abstraction. Review both the successful data path and the failed path as first-class parts of the resulting API.

pitfalls: Expecting a default parameter to replace null.
Passing an extracted method as a callback and losing its receiver.

quiz.explanation: Default parameters activate for undefined, including omitted arguments.

quiz.question: Why can const fn = obj.method; fn() fail?
options: The call no longer supplies obj as the receiver
quiz.explanation: Ordinary this depends on the invocation, so extracting a method loses its object receiver.

lessons.title: Data Modeling Studio
lessons.subtitle: Build a small learning planner with a dependable core.
objectives: Design a normalized model for lessons and progress.
Implement domain operations with explicit invariants.
Evaluate the core using fixtures and a review rubric.

body.heading: Start with the questions the model must answer
paragraphs: A useful model supports the operations your application needs. A learning planner must list lessons, record completion, estimate remaining time, and choose the next session. Separate lesson definitions from learner progress: a title belongs to the curriculum, while completedAt belongs to one learner. Give records stable identifiers and use those identifiers for relationships. This avoids duplicating mutable titles or entire lesson objects inside every progress entry.

Write three realistic fixtures before implementing behavior: a new learner, a learner halfway through a stage, and a learner who has completed everything. Add an intentionally malformed fixture to exercise validation. Inspect whether the model answers each required question without redundant sources of truth. Storing both completedCount and a completion map, for example, creates an obligation to keep them synchronized after every update.

body.heading: Build operations around invariants
paragraphs: An invariant is a rule the model must preserve after every public operation. A completed lesson must exist in the curriculum; duration must be finite and nonnegative; progress for one learner must not mutate another learner. Implement focused operations such as completeLesson, reopenLesson, and planSession. Let each operation validate its inputs before creating a new state or changing owned state according to your chosen policy.

Define selection behavior precisely. A session planner may choose unfinished lessons in curriculum order until its time budget is exhausted. Decide whether an oversized first lesson is skipped, included with a warning, or causes an empty plan. Different policies are defensible, but accidental behavior is not. Use examples that distinguish the policies, including an exact budget fit and a remaining lesson longer than the entire budget.

body.heading: Review the result like a small product
paragraphs: Keep the domain core independent of display and storage so you can exercise it with fixtures. A thin presentation function can produce a readable report containing total lessons, completed lessons, remaining minutes, and the next session. Include an explanation when no session can be planned. This converts internal decisions into behavior that a user can understand and gives you a concrete artifact to review.

Use a weighted rubric: correctness forty percent, clear contracts twenty-five percent, meaningful examples twenty percent, and readable naming fifteen percent. A submission is ready when all invariants hold across the fixtures and another person can explain the update policy from the public functions. Record one design tradeoff and one possible future extension. Avoid adding that extension until the present requirements are complete and the existing model remains easy to inspect.

pitfalls: Duplicating derived totals and forgetting to synchronize them.
Leaving session-budget policy to incidental loop behavior.

lessons.title: Prototypes & the Object Model
lessons.subtitle: Understand the lookup mechanism behind objects and methods.
objectives: Trace property lookup through a prototype chain.
Separate inherited behavior from instance data.
Explain constructor and prototype relationships.

body.heading: Lookup follows a chain
paragraphs: When an object lacks an own property, JavaScript searches its prototype chain until a property is found or the chain ends at null. A prototype is another object, so the same mechanism can repeat through several levels. This shares behavior without copying every method into every instance. A missing property usually produces undefined after the search is exhausted.

Draw an instance with an own title and an inherited describe method. Label where each property lives and where each read finds it. Distinguish the internal prototype relationship from a function's ordinary property named prototype. Object.getPrototypeOf reveals the former. Understanding that distinction prevents the common mistake of treating all properties with similar names as the same mechanism.

body.heading: Reads and writes have different rules
paragraphs: A read can find inherited data, while ordinary assignment often creates an own property that shadows inherited data. Accessors and nonwritable properties introduce additional rules, so inspect descriptors when behavior is surprising. Deleting an own property can reveal an inherited property again. It does not necessarily make every future read of that name return undefined.

Mutable instance data should not accidentally live on a shared prototype. If two learners inherit one history array, pushing through either learner changes the same array. Give each learner an independent array. Shared methods are appropriate because they obtain working state from their receiver. Test both the values and reference identities when diagnosing shared-state bugs.

body.heading: Construction connects identity and behavior
paragraphs: Calling a suitable function with new creates an object, connects its prototype, invokes the constructor with the new receiver, and normally returns that object. Class syntax organizes construction and methods around this prototype-based model. Instances remain ordinary objects with identity and properties; they are not a separate value system disconnected from the rest of JavaScript.

Use prototype inspection for learning and debugging, but avoid changing prototype relationships casually during normal execution. Stable relationships are easier to explain and maintain. Before introducing a class, decide whether the model needs coordinated behavior around an identity or whether a plain record and functions already describe the domain clearly. Shared behavior is a capability, not a requirement for every object. Compare an own-property check with the in operator so your diagram distinguishes storage location from successful lookup through inheritance.

pitfalls: Putting per-instance mutable arrays on a shared prototype.
Confusing an internal prototype with a property named prototype.

quiz.explanation: Instance-specific state needs independent ownership.

quiz.question: Deleting an own property can reveal what?
quiz.explanation: The next read searches the prototype chain.

lessons.title: Classes with Clear Invariants
lessons.subtitle: Design instances whose valid states are easy to understand.
objectives: Establish invariants during construction.
Distinguish static operations from instance methods.
Test valid transitions and rejected operations.

body.heading: Construction establishes valid state
paragraphs: A class groups construction and related behavior under one name. Its constructor should finish with an instance that satisfies the domain rules. A study session might require a positive duration and begin idle. Validate inputs before making the instance available to other code. Avoid implicit network requests or timers during construction when explicit startup would make ownership clearer.

List the fields and the relationships between them. If startedAt is meaningful only while running, every operation must preserve that relationship. Alternatively, choose a representation with fewer impossible combinations. A class earns its place when it coordinates behavior around identity or protects meaningful invariants. Merely wrapping a record in constructor syntax does not automatically improve its design.

body.heading: Methods express transitions
paragraphs: Methods such as start, pause, and complete describe domain transitions more clearly than unrestricted setters for each field. Decide what repeated calls mean: starting an already running session could return its current state or reject the operation. Either policy can work, but callers need a predictable contract. Validate a transition before changing several related fields.

Static methods belong to the class object and can provide named construction helpers such as fromRecord. Getters can expose computed values without storing redundant state. Keep apparently simple reads free of surprising expensive effects. A public surface should let callers distinguish inspection from change and understand which operations can fail before they use the object in a larger workflow.

body.heading: Encapsulation supports change
paragraphs: Encapsulation lets callers rely on a stable interface while internal representation evolves. Naming conventions communicate intent; closures and language features can enforce parts of the boundary. The central question is whether callers can bypass the operations that preserve invariants. If they can create impossible states through public fields, additional validation or a narrower interface is necessary.

Test the class through construction, queries, and transitions. Include malformed constructor inputs and invalid transition sequences. Verify failures leave state unchanged. Tests that rely on every private implementation detail make later improvements difficult, so prefer observable behavior. A strong interface lets you replace a stored derived value with a calculation while keeping callers and their meaningful tests correct. Review each public method against a transition table, including repeated calls and failures, before considering the interface complete.

pitfalls: Exposing setters that bypass domain invariants.
Starting unmanaged resources during construction.

quiz.explanation: Construction establishes invariants that methods must preserve.

quiz.question: Which operation fits a static method?
quiz.explanation: A construction helper operates before a particular instance exists.

lessons.title: Inheritance & Composition
lessons.subtitle: Choose relationships that preserve meaning under change.
objectives: Evaluate subtype behavior against a base contract.
Compose independent policies using collaborators.
Document architecture tradeoffs with concrete changes.

body.heading: Inheritance is a behavioral commitment
paragraphs: A subclass inherits behavior and may override it. The important question is whether a caller expecting the base abstraction can use the subclass without surprising changes. Matching method names is insufficient. Accepted inputs, results, failures, and effects all contribute to the contract. A supposedly general collection that unexpectedly rejects ordinary additions may violate its caller's reasonable expectations.

Write one consumer of the base interface and run it against each proposed subtype. If the consumer needs repeated subtype checks, inspect the hierarchy. Shared fields alone rarely justify inheritance. In a derived constructor, super must initialize the base instance before this is used. Keep initialization responsibilities explicit so state cannot be partially established through an unclear chain of constructor assumptions.

body.heading: Composition separates independent policies
paragraphs: Composition gives an object collaborators instead of encoding every variation in ancestry. A planner can receive a selection strategy and a storage adapter. Changing selection then does not require a new storage subclass, and changing storage does not duplicate selection logic. This matters when two independent choices would otherwise create a growing number of combined subclasses.

Keep collaborator interfaces narrow and behavioral. A selection strategy can simply accept lessons and a budget and return a plan. Specify mutation and failure rules as well as parameter names. Inject a fake collaborator to control outcomes in tests. Avoid creating interfaces for imaginary future changes; extract the boundary when it clarifies a present responsibility or a plausible, concrete variation.

body.heading: Judge the design through a change
paragraphs: Consider adding shortest-first planning and offline storage. Trace which modules change with inheritance and which change with composition. Prefer a structure that keeps independent decisions independent while preserving a readable ordinary call path. More abstractions can increase navigation and configuration costs, so a flexible-looking diagram is not enough evidence that a design is useful.

Write a short decision record with the chosen relationship, the alternatives, and a trigger for reconsideration. Include a situation where inheritance is appropriate, such as a stable extension interface that explicitly expects subclasses. This prevents a guideline from becoming a slogan. The practical objective is predictable behavior for callers and manageable changes for maintainers, demonstrated with examples rather than an elaborate hierarchy.

pitfalls: Using inheritance because records share a few properties.
Creating one subclass for each combination of unrelated policies.

lessons.title: Modules & Public Interfaces
lessons.subtitle: Make dependencies and exported promises visible.
objectives: Define module APIs with explicit exports.
Explain scope and live imported bindings.
Control startup effects at the application boundary.

body.heading: Exports define a vocabulary
paragraphs: A module exposes selected bindings and keeps other declarations local. Exports become the vocabulary other files use to request behavior. A planning module might export planSession and summarizeProgress while retaining its sorting helper privately. Exporting every helper turns implementation choices into accidental promises and makes later refactoring spread across unrelated consumers.

Start with one cohesive responsibility and one usage example per export. Static imports reveal dependencies near the top of a file and help tools analyze the module graph. Runtime loading rules still matter: browser and Node.js projects need compatible paths and configuration. Keep host APIs out of reusable calculations when those calculations should run in more than one environment without special setup.

body.heading: Imports are live bindings
paragraphs: An ES module import remains connected to its exported binding. It is not a detached copy that an importer can reassign freely. If the exporter changes a mutable exported binding, importers can observe that change. This behavior does not make shared mutable exports a good default; unclear ownership still produces difficult interactions across otherwise well-separated files.

Top-level module code can have effects when the module loads. A subscription, timer, or request at import time complicates reuse and testing because a simple dependency declaration now starts work. Export an explicit start or initialize operation when startup needs control. Assign cleanup responsibility for every resource that outlives one call, and make ordinary utility imports predictable.

playground.note: Edit either file. Run example starts app.mjs with real ES module imports; local literal imports only, without circular dependencies.

body.heading: Contracts outlive implementation details
paragraphs: A module interface includes argument shapes, return values, mutation rules, failures, and whether work is asynchronous. Review exports through real consumer examples. If a consumer needs an internal helper only to reconstruct a higher-level operation, the public API may be missing that operation. Alternatively, the files may not represent independent responsibilities yet and can remain together.

Draw the dependency graph and inspect cycles. Circular dependencies are supported in some forms, but initialization and availability can become subtle. Prefer a clear direction when the domain allows it, moving genuinely shared concepts into a lower-level module. A tidy diagram is useful only if the actual contracts remain clear and the boundaries correspond to coherent work that callers need. Keep one runnable consumer example beside the interface documentation so changes can be checked against an actual caller.

pitfalls: Exporting mutable state without ownership rules.
Starting requests or timers during an otherwise ordinary import.

quiz.question: ES module imports are generally what?
quiz.explanation: Imports stay connected to exported bindings.

quiz.question: What improves testable startup?
quiz.explanation: Explicit startup gives applications and tests control.

lessons.title: Dependency Design & Boundaries
lessons.subtitle: Keep the core stable while adapters change.
objectives: Separate domain behavior from environment integration.
Inject narrow storage and clock adapters.
Assign recovery decisions to clear boundaries.

body.heading: Dependency direction shows responsibility
paragraphs: A dependency means one component requires knowledge from another. A calculation that imports the DOM becomes tied to a browser even when its rule has nothing to do with a document. Move environment integration toward the application edge. Let the domain receive ordinary values and return ordinary results, while adapters translate events, storage records, and network messages.

Draw domain, adapter, and startup boxes. Place each existing operation in one box and justify the choice. Startup can connect browser persistence to a pure planner without the planner importing that implementation. Add a layer only when it clarifies a real responsibility or controls a troublesome dependency. Extra indirection without an understandable purpose makes the system harder to navigate.

body.heading: Adapters translate complete contracts
paragraphs: A storage interface needs more than load and save names. Define missing-data behavior, malformed-data errors, synchronous or asynchronous execution, and whether saves replace or merge. An in-memory test adapter should honor the same observable contract as the real one. A fake that always returns success cannot expose the recovery behavior the application promises when persistence fails.

Use shared examples across implementations: save then load preserves the intended record, an unknown key follows the absence policy, and a failed save never claims success. Inject time where it affects decisions. A supplied clock lets examples represent expiry and deadlines without waiting or depending on the computer's current date. These explicit inputs make environmental assumptions reviewable and reproducible.

playground.note: The service and its caller are separate modules. The editable loader is an offline test double, so no account or server is needed.

body.heading: Contain a source of change
paragraphs: Consider replacing local persistence with a remote service. Transport and latency change, and previously synchronous work may become asynchronous. A domain function that already accepts data and returns a plan can remain intact while orchestration changes. If calculations read storage directly, the same transport change spreads through unrelated business logic and increases the number of behaviors you must retest.

Write an architecture note containing the graph, adapter contracts, and one complete sequence. Include failure ownership: the adapter detects malformed storage, orchestration chooses recovery, and the interface communicates the outcome. Avoid logging one error at every layer or leaving recovery to nobody. Review the note against executable examples and remove abstractions whose purpose cannot be demonstrated through a relevant change.

pitfalls: Using a fake adapter with behavior unlike production.
Reading environment state inside domain calculations.

Choose state ownership deliberately.

body.heading: Build a vertical slice
paragraphs: A vertical slice runs from input through domain behavior to a visible result. Give your planner two consumers: a text report and a programmatic interface. Both should call the same domain operations. This proves reuse with working behavior instead of a large collection of abstractions that no caller needs. Keep the first slice small enough to inspect completely.

Write acceptance scenarios for a new learner, partial progress, and a completed curriculum. Each scenario should exercise the real module wiring. Use fixtures whose expected results can be calculated manually. Add one malformed record and verify rejection at the intended boundary. A collection of isolated helper tests cannot prove that the actual application connects those helpers correctly or reports failures coherently.

body.heading: Choose ownership before syntax
paragraphs: Use records for transferable data, functions for calculations, and a class or closure when one identity owns coordinated state. These tools can coexist. A progress store can own persistence while a pure planner calculates recommendations. Do not turn every record into a class to demonstrate syntax; require each abstraction to clarify ownership, preserve invariants, or expose meaningful behavior.

The entry point constructs adapters and connects services. Reusable modules should not secretly import startup state. If a cycle appears, inspect whether responsibilities are entangled or whether a shared concept belongs below both modules. Keep the final graph small enough to explain honestly in one diagram. Omitted dependencies make the diagram prettier but undermine its value as evidence.

body.heading: Prove the design with change
paragraphs: Replace one policy after the first slice works. Switch from curriculum order to shortest-first planning, or replace memory storage with another contract-compatible adapter. Record which modules changed and why. A useful boundary contains the relevant change while unrelated domain behavior remains correct. If edits spread everywhere, repair the dependency direction before adding more features on top of it.

Score correctness at forty percent, boundary clarity at twenty-five, the change demonstration at twenty, and documentation at fifteen. Deliver a run guide, exported API examples, a dependency diagram, and a decision record. Include one limitation and a condition for revisiting the design. The evidence should show that the application solves its current problem and that its abstractions earn their cost.

pitfalls: Treating unused abstractions as proof of flexibility.
Testing helpers without exercising actual module wiring.

lessons.title: The Standard Library Toolkit
lessons.subtitle: Choose collections and binary representations by their behavior.
objectives: Choose Map and Set for appropriate collection semantics.
Distinguish structured data from serialized text.
Recognize when typed arrays and URL objects are useful.

body.heading: Choose a collection by the question
paragraphs: A Set stores unique values and supports membership checks without manually searching an array. A Map associates keys with values and allows keys beyond strings and symbols. Plain objects remain useful for records with known fields. Select the structure by the operations and meaning you need: a lesson record, a set of completed identifiers, and a map from identifier to lesson serve different purposes.

Object keys in a Map use identity, so two equivalent-looking records are still different keys. Set membership has similar identity implications for objects. Prefer stable primitive identifiers when data crosses serialization boundaries. A recreated object will not match the identity of an earlier object merely because their fields agree. Write examples that distinguish duplicate primitives from separately created object values.

body.heading: Serialization changes representation
paragraphs: JSON converts a supported data structure into text and parses text into new values. It does not preserve every JavaScript feature. Functions, undefined values, special numeric values, dates, maps, sets, and cycles require particular care or explicit conversion policies. Parsing successfully only establishes valid JSON syntax; it does not prove that the result matches your application schema or is safe to use.

Treat serialization as a boundary. Define a plain transfer shape, serialize it, parse it, and validate it before creating domain values. Include a version when the shape may evolve. Test round trips using the actual supported values, and do not use JSON serialization as a universal deep-cloning trick. Representation changes can silently remove information that your program depends on.

playground.before: const lessons = [{ id: "L1", title: "Values" }, { id: "L2", title: "Objects" }];

body.heading: Use specialized tools deliberately
paragraphs: Typed arrays provide views of numeric elements over binary memory buffers. They are useful for binary formats, media, and APIs that exchange bytes, while ordinary arrays are more flexible for general application records. URL and URLSearchParams provide structured handling of addresses and query parameters, avoiding fragile string concatenation and manual escaping. Specialized tools reduce errors when their contracts match the problem.

Explore one tool at a time with a small concrete example: deduplicate completion IDs, index lessons by ID, serialize a progress record, and build a shareable filter URL. Explain the input and output representation at each step. Avoid selecting a sophisticated collection merely for novelty; the best choice makes the expected operations and identity rules obvious to the next reader.

pitfalls: Using object identity when stable IDs are needed across loads.
Assuming valid JSON is valid application data.

quiz.explanation: A Set directly expresses uniqueness and membership.

quiz.question: What does successful JSON.parse guarantee?
quiz.explanation: The parsed value still needs domain validation.

lessons.title: Text, Dates & Internationalization
lessons.subtitle: Handle patterns, time, and presentation without hidden assumptions.
objectives: Use regular expressions for bounded text patterns.
Separate timestamps from localized presentation.
Format numbers and dates using explicit locale decisions.

body.heading: Patterns are small parsers with limits
paragraphs: A regular expression describes a pattern in text. Anchors constrain where a match occurs, character classes describe allowed characters, and quantifiers specify repetition. Use a regex when the pattern is small and understandable. Complex nested data or a rich grammar usually deserves a parser. A concise pattern is not automatically readable, correct, or safe for every input size.

Write accepted and rejected examples before the pattern, including empty input and boundary lengths. Decide whether the entire string must match or whether a substring is enough. Flags change behavior, and global or sticky expressions maintain lastIndex state across relevant operations. Avoid reusing a stateful regex casually as if every test were independent. Explain each part of the pattern in ordinary language.

body.heading: A timestamp is not a calendar policy
paragraphs: A Date represents an instant as a numeric time value, while its formatting and component access can depend on a time zone. Calendar dates, local appointment times, and elapsed durations are different concepts. Adding a fixed number of milliseconds is suitable for an elapsed duration but may not implement a local calendar-day rule around daylight-saving transitions or other offset changes.

Store and exchange timestamps in an explicit format, and decide which time zone the product uses for calendar interpretation. Avoid ambiguous date strings whose parsing assumptions are unclear. Inject the current time into rules so boundary tests are deterministic. Include examples near midnight and a relevant offset transition when a feature promises calendar behavior rather than simply measuring elapsed milliseconds.

body.heading: Presentation belongs at a boundary
paragraphs: Intl formatters express locale-sensitive number and date presentation without manually assembling punctuation or month names. Keep domain values numeric or structured until the presentation boundary. A formatted currency string is a display value, not a reliable input for arithmetic. Likewise, do not compare localized date strings to decide which event occurred first; compare appropriate time values instead.

Create reusable formatters for a chosen locale and explicit time zone when consistency matters. Compare two locales to observe differences in grouping, decimal separators, and date order. Your tests should distinguish semantic correctness from exact presentation expectations. Record whether a product follows the viewer's preferences or an organization-wide setting so the same timestamp does not appear mysteriously inconsistent across screens.

pitfalls: Treating localized display strings as arithmetic or sorting values.
Assuming an elapsed twenty-four hours always means the next local calendar day.

quiz.question: What should be compared to order instants?
quiz.explanation: Numeric timestamps represent chronological order without locale formatting ambiguity.

quiz.question: Why can a reused global regex surprise you?
quiz.explanation: Global and sticky expressions can retain position state between operations.

lessons.title: Iterators & Generators
lessons.subtitle: Process sequences lazily through a shared protocol.
objectives: Distinguish an iterable from an iterator.
Use generators to express lazy sequences.
Explain exhaustion and cleanup during iteration.

body.heading: Iteration is a protocol
paragraphs: An iterable supplies a method at Symbol.iterator that returns an iterator. An iterator supplies next, whose result describes a value and whether iteration is done. for...of and spread consume this protocol. A collection can create a fresh iterator for each traversal, while an iterator commonly represents one evolving position. These are related roles, not interchangeable guarantees of repeatable iteration.

Inspect a built-in iterator manually by calling next several times. Record the value and done fields, including the exhausted state. Then compare consuming the same iterator twice with requesting a new iterator from the original collection. This experiment explains why a function accepting an arbitrary iterable should not assume it can traverse the input repeatedly without documenting that requirement.

body.heading: Generators describe suspended computation
paragraphs: A generator function returns a generator object when called. Its body advances when the consumer requests the next item, suspending at yield. Local variables remain available between resumptions, which makes stateful sequence logic readable. A range generator can produce values without first allocating an array for the entire range. Laziness changes when work happens and can reduce memory requirements.

Laziness does not automatically make every algorithm faster. Repeated consumption may repeat computation, and a consumer that spreads an infinite generator into an array never finishes. Define whether a sequence is finite and how a consumer can stop. Use generators when the incremental nature of the data improves the model, such as traversing pages or producing records as they become available.

body.heading: Composition needs termination and cleanup
paragraphs: Generator helpers can map, filter, or limit a sequence while preserving lazy evaluation. A take helper should consume only the requested number of items and handle zero cleanly. Early termination matters when the source owns resources. Iteration protocols can support cleanup through return, and a generator can use try/finally to release resources when consumption closes it appropriately.

Build an instrumented source that logs each produced value, then apply a filter and a limit. Compare the produced count with the returned count; filtering may require examining more items than the output contains. Document this distinction when work is expensive. Test empty input, exhaustion, early stopping, and a consumer exception so your abstraction does not accidentally promise a simpler lifecycle than it implements.

pitfalls: Assuming every iterator can be restarted.
Materializing an unbounded sequence with spread.

quiz.question: What does calling a generator function immediately return?
quiz.explanation: The generator object advances its body as iteration requests values.

quiz.question: Why distinguish iterable from iterator?
options: An iterable can provide fresh traversal while an iterator tracks progress
quiz.explanation: A sequence source and one traversal state have different lifecycle properties.

practice.prompt: Implement generator-based map and take helpers.

practice.title: Production audit
practice.prompt: Instrument a filtered sequence and measure produced versus returned values.

recap: Iteration is a shared protocol.
Generators suspend computation between requests.
Laziness needs explicit termination assumptions.

lessons.title: Promises & Failure Semantics
lessons.subtitle: Reason about eventual values and connected error paths.
objectives: Trace fulfillment, rejection, and chained promises.
Return asynchronous work so callers can observe it.
Distinguish recovery from accidental error swallowing.

body.heading: A promise represents an eventual outcome
paragraphs: A promise begins pending and eventually fulfills with a value or rejects with a reason. Its state settles once. Attaching handlers observes that outcome without blocking the current stack. A promise is not the result itself, and creating one does not automatically move CPU work onto another thread. The surrounding API determines what work occurs and how it is scheduled.

Draw a timeline with synchronous statements and promise reactions. Handlers run after the current synchronous work completes according to the host's scheduling model. Predict a simple log order before running it. Keep the distinction between starting an operation and observing its promise: a request may already be in flight before you attach a handler or pass the promise to another function.

body.heading: Chains connect values and failures
paragraphs: then returns a new promise. Returning a plain value fulfills that next promise with the value; returning a promise adopts its eventual outcome. Throwing inside a handler rejects the next promise. This is why return is essential when a handler begins another asynchronous operation. Without it, the outer chain may finish before the nested work and cannot reliably observe its result or failure.

Keep each step focused on one transformation. Name the intermediate result and specify whether it is immediate or eventual. A catch handler that returns a value converts rejection into fulfillment, which is a recovery policy. If recovery is impossible, rethrow or let the rejection propagate. Logging an error and returning nothing can accidentally make a failed operation appear successfully completed with undefined.
body.code:
loadProgress()
  .then(progress => savePlan(buildPlan(progress)))
  .then(() => console.log("Saved"))
  .catch(error => console.error("Plan failed:", error.message));

body.heading: Completion and cleanup are different concerns
paragraphs: finally is useful for cleanup that should happen after fulfillment or rejection. It does not receive the successful value or rejection reason as its argument. A failure thrown during cleanup can replace the earlier outcome, so cleanup deserves its own contract. Avoid using finally to manufacture success or to hide an error that the caller still needs to handle.

At the application boundary, attach a deliberate rejection path. Record what the user sees, which diagnostics remain available, and whether retry is appropriate. Test a failure at each asynchronous step rather than only rejecting the first request. The chain should connect all work that belongs to the operation, and its returned promise should settle only when the operation's promised responsibility is complete.

pitfalls: Starting nested async work without returning its promise.
Catching a failure and unintentionally converting it into success.

quiz.question: What happens when a then handler throws?
quiz.explanation: Thrown handler errors become rejections in the chained promise.

quiz.question: What does returning a fallback from catch do?
options: Recovers into fulfillment with that value
quiz.explanation: A normal return from catch produces a fulfilled continuation.

practice.prompt: Predict and verify a mixed synchronous and promise log sequence.
success: The current stack is distinguished from reactions.

practice.prompt: Repair nested asynchronous work whose promise is not returned.

practice.title: Recovery policy
practice.prompt: Implement one recoverable failure and one propagated failure.

Return work to connect the chain.

lessons.title: Async Workflows & Concurrency
lessons.subtitle: Control overlap, failure, and cancellation deliberately.
objectives: Use async/await without losing error semantics.
Choose sequential or concurrent execution intentionally.
Bound concurrency and handle stale results.

body.heading: Await makes suspension readable
paragraphs: An async function always returns a promise. await pauses that function's continuation until its operand settles, while other work can proceed in the environment. A rejection at await behaves like a thrown error inside the async function and can be handled with try/catch. This syntax makes asynchronous control flow resemble ordinary sequencing, but it does not turn an eventual result into a synchronous return value.

Trace both the caller and callee. Calling an async function gives the caller a promise immediately; awaiting it connects the caller's continuation to the outcome. Avoid mixing awaited and unobserved work accidentally. If a background operation is intentional, give it its own failure handling and lifecycle. Otherwise return or await it so the function's promise accurately represents the responsibility its name suggests.

body.heading: Overlap independent work deliberately
paragraphs: Sequential awaits are appropriate when a later step depends on an earlier result. Independent operations can be started together and observed with Promise.all. Promise.all rejects when one input rejects, but it does not cancel the remaining work. Promise.allSettled collects every outcome when partial results are useful. Choose the combinator from the product's failure policy rather than treating concurrency as an automatic speed improvement.

Unbounded concurrency can overload a service or consume too much memory. A worker pool limits the number of active operations while preserving a defined output order. Separate concurrency, rate limits, and total work: limiting active requests does not necessarily limit requests per second. Start with a small pool and instrument active counts so the bound is supported by evidence instead of assumed from the code.

body.heading: Cancellation and stale results need ownership
paragraphs: Cancellation is cooperative: an operation must support and observe a cancellation signal. Aborting a request does not retroactively undo every side effect or settle unrelated work. A browser search interface also needs stale-result protection, because an earlier request can finish after a newer one. Use a request identity or equivalent state check before committing a response to current UI state.

Test timing with controlled deferred promises rather than relying on random delays. Resolve requests in reverse order, reject one worker, and cancel an operation while another is active. Specify whether partial results are retained and what cleanup occurs. These examples expose race conditions that a normal fast connection often hides, and they turn concurrency from a vague performance feature into an explicit behavioral contract.

pitfalls: Assuming Promise.all cancels remaining operations after rejection.
Letting an older request overwrite newer interface state.

quiz.question: When one Promise.all input rejects, what is guaranteed?
quiz.explanation: The aggregate rejects, but ongoing operations are not automatically canceled.

quiz.question: Why use a request identity in live search?
options: To prevent stale responses from replacing newer results
quiz.explanation: An identity check connects a response to the currently relevant request.

practice.prompt: Process a collection with a concurrency limit of three.

practice.prompt: Resolve two searches in reverse order.
